text: What causes wars and quarrels among you? Isn't it this: your cravings that wage war inside you?

versions.text: What causes the wars and the fights among you? Isn't it this: your cravings that wage war within you?
versions.explanation: The Greek nouns are anarthrous; the definite articles ("the wars and the fights") make the question sound as if specific conflicts were already mentioned. "Quarrels" better distinguishes μάχαι from πόλεμοι, and dropping the articles improves the rhythm for oral reading.

text: You want and do not have, so you kill. You covet and cannot obtain, so you quarrel and fight. You do not have because you do not ask.
And when you ask, you do not receive, because you ask with wrong motives—to spend it on your own pleasures.
You adulterous people! Don't you know that friendship with the world is hostility toward God? So whoever chooses to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God.

versions.text: You adulterers! Don't you know that friendship with the world is hostility toward God? So whoever chooses to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God.
versions.explanation: μοιχαλίδες is feminine ("adulteresses"), drawing on the prophetic image of God's unfaithful bride. "You adulterers" reads as a literal accusation of marital infidelity against men; "You adulterous people" preserves the metaphor of spiritual unfaithfulness without misleading the hearer.

text:
Or do you think Scripture speaks in vain when it says that the spirit God made to dwell in us yearns with envy?[^1]

[^1]: Or, "God yearns jealously over the spirit he made to dwell in us." The Greek can be read either way.

versions.text: Or do you think Scripture speaks in vain when it says that the spirit God made to dwell in us yearns with envy?
versions.explanation: This clause is one of the most disputed in the letter; the alternative reading takes God (or the Spirit) as the one who longs jealously. A brief footnote alerts the hearer to the ambiguity without altering the chosen rendering.

text: But he gives greater grace. That is why it says: "God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble."
So submit yourselves to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.
Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Wash your hands, you sinners, and purify your hearts, you double-minded.
Be miserable, mourn, and weep. Let your laughter be turned to mourning and your joy to gloom.

versions.text: Grieve, mourn, and weep. Let your laughter be turned to mourning and your joy to gloom.
versions.explanation: ταλαιπωρήσατε means "be wretched/miserable," a distinct call to feel the misery of sin; "grieve" overlaps almost entirely with "mourn" (πενθήσατε) in the next word, flattening the triad into a redundancy.

text: Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will lift you up.
Brothers, do not slander one another. Whoever slanders a brother or judges his brother slanders the law and judges the law. And if you judge the law, you are not a doer of the law but its judge.
There is only one lawgiver and judge, the one who is able to save and to destroy. But you—who are you to judge your neighbor?

versions.text: There is only one lawgiver and judge, the one who is able to save and to destroy. So who are you to judge your neighbor?
versions.explanation: The δέ here is sharply contrastive, setting the single divine Judge over against the presumptuous human judge, and the emphatic σύ is fronted in Greek. "So" reads as a mild inference and loses the rhetorical punch of the confrontation.

text: Now listen, you who say, "Today or tomorrow we will go to this or that city, spend a year there, do business, and make a profit."
You do not even know what tomorrow will bring, or what your life will be. You are a mist that appears for a little while and then vanishes.
Instead you ought to say, "If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that."
As it is, you boast in your arrogance. All such boasting is evil.
So then, if anyone knows the good he ought to do and does not do it, it is sin for him.
